articles.title: Vice-presidente da Indonésia renuncia após polêmica acadêmica | G1
articles.standfirst: Tribunais decidiram que documentos apresentados sobre estudos no exterior não atendiam aos requisitos eleitorais.
articles.summary: Vice-presidente da Indonésia, Gibran Rakabuming Raka renuncia após tribunais invalidarem seus diplomas e parlamentares iniciarem processo de impeachment.
articles.body:
O vice-presidente da Indonésia, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, deixa o prédio do Parlamento após apresentar sua carta de renúncia em Jacarta. — Foto: Tatan Syuflana / AP

O vice-presidente da Indonésia renunciou nesta quinta-feira (12), em meio ao aumento dos questionamentos sobre sua elegibilidade para o cargo, após decisões judiciais recentes colocarem em dúvida suas credenciais educacionais.

Gibran Rakabuming Raka, de 39 anos, filho do ex-presidente Joko Widodo, apresentou sua renúncia à direção da Assembleia Consultiva do Povo, o mais alto órgão legislativo do país, no prédio do Parlamento, na capital, Jacarta.

Raka não fez comentários ao deixar a reunião.

A investigação sobre suas credenciais acadêmicas aparentemente não tinha relação com as investigações sobre alegações de que altos funcionários da polícia estariam envolvidos em escutas telefônicas contra o presidente.

Segundo a Constituição da Indonésia, a vacância do cargo de vice-presidente não provoca uma nova eleição. O cargo permanece vago até que a Assembleia Consultiva do Povo eleja um substituto entre dois candidatos indicados pelo presidente no prazo de 60 dias.

Raka havia se oferecido para renunciar na terça-feira, durante uma reunião com o presidente Prabowo Subianto, afirmando que queria evitar uma controvérsia política prolongada. Mas um ministro do governo disse que, na ocasião, o presidente pediu a Raka que se defendesse, e não ficou claro se ele havia aceitado o pedido de renúncia.

O Tribunal Constitucional e a Suprema Corte decidiram no mês passado que os documentos apresentados por Raka sobre sua formação no exterior não atendiam aos requisitos eleitorais.

Uma petição posterior, apresentada na quarta-feira à liderança da Câmara por 120 parlamentares de oito partidos políticos, deu início a um processo parlamentar que poderia levar ao seu impeachment.

Segundo a legislação indonésia, os líderes da Câmara devem criar uma comissão especial para avaliar se Raka violou a Constituição ao exercer o cargo de vice-presidente apesar de supostamente não cumprir os requisitos eleitorais. Se os parlamentares concluírem que há fundamentos suficientes para a acusação, a Câmara deverá pedir ao Tribunal Constitucional que decida se houve uma violação da Constituição.

articles.title: 'You're triggering me': How to understand your therapy-speak teen
articles.summary: Words most often heard in the therapist's chair have made their way into day-to-day conversation - here's a parents' guide to understanding it.
articles.body:
With claims of gaslighting, triggering and disrespecting boundaries, some parents are struggling to understand their teenagers' so-called therapy speak.

When Carla Hoskins asks her 15 and 18-year-old sons to revise or do chores at their Hertfordshire home, she says she is sometimes met with: "You're triggering me!"

Over in the US, Shannon Salvatoriello says her 14 and 17-year-old sons use similar words, which she says leaves her "feeling very confused".

Mental health experts in the UK and US tell the BBC why young people are using terms often heard during therapy sessions in everyday conversation - and give parents tips on how to better understand their teenagers.

Mum-of-six Carla says she is sometimes accused of gaslighting by her teen sons - particularly when she asks about friends or schoolwork.

"I feel like any time you challenge them or request something is when you come up against this new language," says the 39-year-old.

"Rather than just saying, 'Mum, I'm stressed about my exams' or 'I've got a lot on my plate', it's I'm triggering them." She adds: "You can't really ever get to the bottom of anything."

Carla says she had never heard the words triggering or gaslighting before her sons started using them and assumes they learned them on social media.

New York psychiatrist Dr Suzanne Garfinkle-Crowell agrees this is one of the ways therapy speak has spread to everyday language. Social media is one of the places teenagers look to as they try to make sense of themselves and the world, she says.

She has observed a shift in the way young people talk about their problems - from describing their feelings to giving them labels, she tells BBC Radio 4’s Woman’s Hour .

"They would say, 'I'm not getting along with my mum'... 'School has gotten really challenging and I'm feeling kind of bad about myself', and then suddenly it was, 'I have attachment issues, ADHD, and depression'."

Garfinkle-Crowell says parents shouldn't be afraid to consult a mental health professional if their child is describing symptoms of a medical condition, like anxiety disorder or depression.

She understands that some parents feel the use of therapy speak by teens is "almost like they are speaking a new language", but says it is important they consider the backdrop to why they might be using it.

Many young people, and girls in particular, often feel they aren't taken seriously by their parents and society more generally, she says.

"The only way to feel heard is to reach for this elevated medical language."

The head of an independent review into youth mental health told BBC News in September it was "harder to be young" now. Prof Peter Fonagy said there had been a real rise in mental distress among young people given the economic and employment uncertainty their generation faces.

However, Julia Samuel, a psychotherapist from London, warns young people using medical terms such as anxiety disorder to describe "normal feelings like mild distress" can create a pattern of behaviour and emotions that result in them developing a disorder.

"It can give them the very thing they don't want," she explains. "It's the lack of knowledge and the overuse of the terms that can actually harm young people."

Samuel says for parents struggling to understand therapy speak, "listening is your biggest tool to bridge the divide".

She then suggests using "ordinary emotional language to reflect back" what your teenager is saying to help you understand what they are feeling.

Garfinkle-Crowell agrees a helpful technique for parents is to think about the words you would associate with the therapy term a teen is using.

"You may try offering [something] like, 'That sounds like it could be really lonely for you. Is that part of it?'" she says.

"You're really trying to consider [their] experience," she says. "You're [also] not making it worse - by not overreacting or under-reacting - you're just being present."

Mum-of-four Shannon, from New Jersey, says it took her several years to learn her approach of "I'm your parent and I'm asking you a question and you are going to answer me" was not helpful for her teenagers.

She became frustrated when they would push back - sometimes using phrases about her not respecting their boundaries.

Samuel says carefully choosing when and how you talk to your teenager can help them talk more openly, instead of hiding behind therapy speak.

Rather than asking them in a direct manner, she suggests talking about yourself being in a similar situation.

"You could bring up a subject about yourself at school or something that's related... so it isn't kind of pointing a finger at them," she says.

Shannon says: "I've noticed when I do back off they will then come to me later to say, 'Hey, guess what? I got a 95 on that Spanish test'... You don't have to ask them for three days straight about something."

Carla is glad she's open with her teenagers and feels they can discuss things with her - even if she sometimes struggles with the meaning.

"We are close and I think that's why sometimes they think that they can use these [therapy] words, as if they're talking to a friend."

If you or someone you know is experiencing mental or emotional distress, you can access support from the BBC Action Line .

articles.title: Netanyahu asks military to prepare for Iran 2.0 as opposition demands no strikes before next govt
articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's security cabinet on Wednesday directed the military to prepare for a possible renewed attack on Iran, as
articles.body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's security cabinet on Wednesday directed the military to prepare for a possible renewed attack on Iran, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot urged the caretaker government to avoid unnecessary military operations until a new administration takes office.“The directives issued by the security cabinet to the Israeli military could lead it to carry out activities that could trigger a war,” Israeli public broadcaster KAN reported.The security cabinet had last met on October 5, weeks before elections were held on October 27. The latest directives were publicised after Eisenkot called on Netanyahu to exercise restraint during the political transition.In a letter to Netanyahu, Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming Israel's next government, warned against launching military or security operations unless there was an immediate threat, Israeli media reported.According to the Ynet news website, Eisenkot said Netanyahu was leading a caretaker government that no longer enjoyed the confidence of the Knesset, Israel's parliament.“Only 46 Knesset members still support your continued tenure as prime minister,” he said.In a post shared on X, Eisenkot said Netanyahu had a responsibility to exercise particular caution while taking security and national decisions during the transition period.“The deployment of security forces without a direct and immediate threat that cannot be delayed could have devastating consequences for Israeli democracy and public trust in government institutions,” he warned.He urged Netanyahu to demonstrate restraint and avoid “dangerous moves” that could wait until a new government backed by the Knesset was sworn in.Israeli President Isaac Herzog formally tasked Eisenkot with forming the next government on Sunday after parliamentary factions representing 67 lawmakers recommended him. A total of 46 lawmakers backed Netanyahu, while seven declined to recommend either candidate, Anadolu Ajansi reported.Eisenkot has 28 days to form a governing coalition, with a possible 14-day extension.You use AI every day. articles.title: After killing ex-Tech Mahindra regional head Paramjeet Dhankar, accused shouted, ‘Happy Diwali, I will kill whole family today’
articles.summary: FARIDABAD: “Happy Diwali.
articles.body: FARIDABAD: “Happy Diwali. I will kill the whole family today,” Mohan Sharma allegedly shouted after shooting his neighbour, former Tech Mahindra regional business head Paramjeet Dhankhar, dead in Faridabad.A woman relative tried to stop him, but Sharma continued firing on the road while hurling abuses. CCTV footage also showed him reloading his weapon with another magazine.A day before the murder, Sharma had allegedly been involved in an altercation with Dhankhar and his friends. Sharma was arrested by a Crime Branch team near DLF Chowk in Ballabhgarh the following day.A police investigation has revealed that the former senior IT executive and his friends abused Sharma, leaving him humiliated and nursing a grudge that eventually culminated in the murder on Nov 6. Sharma, a scrap dealer, was arrested within hours of the murder.A senior police officer said the hostility between the two families had escalated after Dhankar’s family lodged a complaint against Sharma with police a few days before the murder.The confrontation, later on, involving Dhankar and his friends, after he returned to India, aggravated the situation.Dhankar, who hailed from Hisar and was based in Singapore, had returned to Faridabad on Nov 5 to attend his nephew’s wedding, scheduled for Nov 24. He is survived by his wife, son, daughter and parents.The autopsy report confirmed that Dhankar sustained nine bullet injuries.The 45-year-old senior vice-president at Singapore-based FPT Software Company Ltd and former regional business head of Tech Mahindra’s Asia-Pacific operations collapsed on the road outside his house in Faridabad Sector 21C on Friday night.Sharma allegedly decided to eliminate Dhankar after he could not bear the insult. According to an officer, the accused deliberately called Dhankar downstairs on the pretext of asking him to move his car, while carrying his licensed .45 ACP pistol fitted with an extended magazine. He then opened fire, pumping 14 rounds at Dhankar and his son, nine of which struck the senior executive.The officer said, “During interrogation, Sharma revealed that he could not bear the insult and decided to shoot Dhankar. The accused had nursed a grudge against the victim after being humiliated a day before the murder. He intentionally called him downstairs with the intention of killing him.”Police have recovered the weapon used in the murder from Sharma, who remains in police custody for further interrogation. Investigators are examining the sequence of events leading to the shooting, including the altercation a day earlier and the circumstances in which the accused allegedly planned and executed the attack.On Friday night, Sharma allegedly rang the doorbell of Dhankar’s house and asked him to come downstairs to move his car. Dhankar’s son Shaurya accompanied him to the parking area. An argument broke out, following which Sharma pulled out his pistol and opened fire at close range after around four minutes’ conversation.After talking for around four minutes, the accused opened fire at him and continued to fire even after the victim fell on the ground.The victim tried to escape and close the gate of the building from outside but the accused chased him out also and then again fired multiple shots at him.He also fired at Shaurya, who managed to escape by taking cover behind parked vehicles. Dhankar collapsed at the spot and died before he could be taken to hospital. The investigation has also brought into focus the history of disputes between the two families, who lived in the same building.Their disagreements included parking issues and a dispute over Sharma’s pet dog defecating in the common parking area. Dhankar’s family had also complained about alleged abuse and damage to their house gate. Police registered a case under sections 103 (murder), 109 (attempt to murder) and 61(2) (criminal conspiracy) of BNS.Stay updated with the latest Faridabad news. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Australian teen missing in bush for six days rescued alive
articles.summary: The 17-year-old's mum has joked that he is "grounded for life" and "never leaving the house again".
articles.body:
A teenager missing for six days in dense Australian bushland has been found alive.

William, whose surname has not been released, disappeared last Friday while on a camping trip with a friend in bushland about 180km (112 miles) east of Melbourne, Victoria.

Extremely cold overnight temperatures had left authorities concerned for the 17-year-old's welfare. Police dogs, divers and helicopters had been involved in the search.

He was located on Thursday morning and reunited with his relieved family, who said he was uninjured but "grounded for life".

Rescuers winched William to safety, and fed him a doughnut and a bottle of water, before he was taken to hospital for a check up.

The boy's mother, Elizabeth Barkley, told reporters the teenager had "only a few scratches" and seemed fit and healthy.

"He's doing fine, everything seems to be fine, he's in perfect health," she added.

"He just stayed in one spot and waited to be rescued and I'm just over the moon he's alive."

Joking, she added: "He's never leaving the house again."

Police have said officers were emotional to have found the teen alive.

"It doesn't happen all the time," Victoria Police Acting Inspector Jason Benbow said. "I'm sure he's got a story to tell us soon, which we're very keen to hear," he added.

articles.title: 'Stop anti-India hate': Indian-American Congressman-elect Amish Shah lists top priorities
articles.summary: Indian-American Congressman-elect Amish Shah has said that tackling anti-India hate in the United States and restoring Congress's authority over tariffs
articles.body: Indian-American Congressman-elect Amish Shah has said that tackling anti-India hate in the United States and restoring Congress's authority over tariffs will be among his top priorities when he takes office on January 3.Amish Shah said he wants to take tariff-related powers away from the White House and give Congress a greater role in decisions on trade.Speaking to news agency ANI on the sidelines of a press conference organised by the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus (CAPAC) on Wednesday (local time), Amish Shah said members of the Indian-American community had raised concerns about anti-India hate and the impact of tariffs on Indian entrepreneurs and businesses."One of the top priorities that the Indian American community told me about, besides stopping Indian hate, is that they also talked clearly about how the tariffs were hurting our Indian entrepreneurs and the Indian business community," Shah told ANI.He said rolling back tariffs and restoring Congress's authority over such decisions would also benefit small businesses, including those in his constituency."Rolling back those tariffs, reasserting Congress's authority over tariffs, and taking it away from the White House will be a top priority as well. We want to help all the small businesses, including all the ones in my district," he said.Shah also pointed out that tariffs were making basic goods more expensive for American consumers, adding that the incoming Congress would work to address the issue."You cannot have these basic things cost more for the American people out there because of these tariffs. We are going to be the ones who have to stop that," Shah told ANI.Plans to join India CaucusAmish Shah said he planned to join the India Caucus in Congress and referred to Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi and other members expected to be present when the new Congress begins its work on January 3."I plan to join the India caucus. Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, and so there are six members who will be present on January 3rd," he said.Healthcare, economy and water supply among prioritiesApart from issues concerning the Indian-American community, Shah outlined several domestic priorities, including the rising cost of living, the economy, affordable healthcare, access to insurance coverage and water supply in his district."The American people made it very clear that they want us to focus on costs, the economy, health care and bringing down those premiums and covering everybody. People of my district sent me here because we are also worried about our water supply. All of those are our top priorities here, as well as tackling the corruption we have seen over the last couple of years that has caused economic hardship," Amish Shah said.He said the incoming lawmakers would begin working on the issues raised by voters from their first day in office."We have not forgotten the clear message that was sent, and that is going to be what we are going to do on day one, January 3rd," he said.Shah, a Democrat, defeated Republican Jay Feely in the 2026 midterm elections to win Arizona's 1st Congressional District. He became the first South Asian American to represent Arizona in the US Congress.According to CNN's election results updated on November 10, with an estimated 99% of votes counted, Shah secured 52.4% of the vote, while Feely received 45.4%.You use AI every day. articles.title: G7 members raise alarm over China's activities near Taiwan
articles.summary: The Group of seven (G7) foreign ministers have warned that China's increasingly assertive activities in the waters off Taiwan's eastern coast pose a
articles.body: The Group of seven (G7) foreign ministers have warned that China's increasingly assertive activities in the waters off Taiwan's eastern coast pose a threat to regional stability, freedom of navigation and international shipping safety.In a joint declaration issued late Wednesday following a meeting in Paris, the ministers underlined the need to preserve peace and stability across the Taiwan strait and opposed any unilateral attempts to alter the existing situation through force, coercion or threats, according to news agency Reuters.China, which considers Taiwan part of its territory, has intensified its activities off the island's eastern coast since June, conducting regular patrols by its coast guard. Taiwanese officials, however, believe Beijing is using these operations to prepare for a possible maritime blockade by deploying a combination of military, paramilitary and civilian vessels.The G7 statement said China's increasingly assertive actions in the waters east of Taiwan threatened regional stability, freedom of navigation and the safety of international shipping."We reaffirmed our opposition to any unilateral attempts to change the status quo, particularly by force or coercion, or the threat thereof," the ministers said.China's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Beijing does not recognise Taiwan's claims of sovereignty and maintains that the self-governed island is part of its territory.Following the Chinese coast guard's latest patrol off Taiwan's eastern coast last month, Taipei accused Beijing of harassing commercial vessels and attempting to impose what it described as an illegitimate maritime jurisdiction.Taiwan considers the waters off its eastern coast strategically important, as they could serve as vital supply routes for assistance from international allies in the event of a military conflict or blockade.The United States, Britain, France and Germany have previously raised concerns over China's activities in the region.Meanwhile, China's military continues to maintain a regular presence around Taiwan. articles.title: In 1975, a Nebraska shop owner buried a Chevy Vega with thousands of keepsakes; 50 years later, his daughter opened the vault and found the car remarkably preserved
articles.summary: After 50 years underground, a daughter uncovers a remarkably preserved Chevy Vega and thousands of mementoes left by her father, a Nebraska store owner, revealing heartfelt letters and nostalgic items from 1975.
articles.body: Most people like the idea of leaving something behind for their grandchildren, a window into how life was back then. Harold Davisson, a Seward, Nebraska, furniture store owner, did something similar. He left a brand new car to sit underground for half a century. On July 4, 1975, he sealed a yellow Chevrolet Vega in a concrete vault filled with thousands of mementoes. Nebraska Public Media reported that his daughter, Trish Johnson, counted more than 5,000 items in the vault. She opened it in 2025, and the car inside was in remarkably good shape.A hometown store owner with a giant planSeward resident Tobin Beck called Davisson “Bud.” Beck said Davisson was an upbeat and community-minded individual who was good at selling his town. Johnson recalled that her father once had an opportunity to relocate his store to another town where he would earn much more. He, however, decided to stay. Her father wanted his grandchildren to be able to recall what it was like in 1975, Johnson told NBC News. So, he built a 45-ton concrete vault underground. Then he put a new Vega, listed as having no mileage, as well as a Kawasaki motorcycle. Other items include a pet rock, a Teflon skillet, and a Barbie doll. Davisson died in 1999, but he had left instructions that the vault should be opened on its 50th anniversary.Letters to the future The vault held more than just cars and toys. It also included letters from hundreds of Seward residents. Kathy and Steve Hartman were a young couple back in 1975. Kathy wrote letters for Steve and her future children. When the capsule opened, she received a letter from her mother, Della, who died eight years ago. Kathy knew the handwriting immediately. The envelope itself made her cry, she said. Inside, her mother wrote that the family liked Steve and was pretty sure Kathy would marry him. At 21, Beck wrote a two-page letter to his future children. Kathy said that in some ways it seems like it was just yesterday and in other ways it feels like a very long time ago.How the Vega held up Opening the vault took three days, during which hundreds of people visited Seward to see the treasures. The Drive reported that the Vega was under a plastic sheet, with a few rust patches on the hood. Davisson made sure to build a ventilation system to keep the moisture out. Unfortunately, the paper was not as good. Johnson explained that there was a mould-like growth on the outside of the paper and cardboard materials. There were numerous plastic-wrapped packages in good condition. She expected about 80% of people would get their items back, but the rest would be disappointed. One man from Virginia found a letter from his mother. A woman from Colorado came to retrieve a cassette recording of her family’s voices.What experts say about sealed time The mixed result matches what experts say about time capsules. The US National Archives explains that success depends on the container, the seal, and the air inside it. It also depends on what items are selected and on any living thing that grows in the right conditions. The summary of R.L. Barclay’s paper, ‘Notes on Time Capsules,’ mentions that the inside should keep out as much oxygen and water as possible. It also says that acidic paper can influence the air around it. The family lost the title of the world's largest time capsule in 1983. They later added a pyramid over the vault to win it back. It sat on top of the sealed vault, so the vault itself stayed shut until 2025. Chris Galen, who travelled from Virginia, told NBC News that the capsule is about who people were in 1975 and who they are now.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: New York building collapse kills at least two, officials say
articles.summary: A dangerous search for survivors continues after a three-storey building collapsed in Brooklyn on Wednesday afternoon.
articles.body:
At least two people have died and more than 17 others are injured after a building in New York City collapsed into an open construction site, officials have said.

It sparked a massive search-and-rescue operation, with more than 250 first responders at the scene in Brooklyn, trying to find survivors who may have been trapped under the rubble of the three-storey building.

Hours later, aerial video showed firefighters pulling a survivor, covered in dust, out of the debris on a stretcher.

Authorities are yet to determine what caused the sudden collapse at about 16:00 local time (21:00 GMT) on Wednesday.

The rescue mission has been described as "extremely dangerous" by New York City Fire Department (FDNY) Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore.

She added that people from the collapsed building and also the construction site had been trapped.

"Members have been working methodically and haven't stopped since they arrived this afternoon," Bonsignore said.

Some pictures of the collapsed building, on Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn, show an entire side of it gone, with bedrooms and closets exposed. Among the debris, smashed concrete and twisted metal, are household items and clothes.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani joined emergency responders at the scene, praising them for their rapid response.

They "arrived in under a minute and have spent hours working in dangerous and highly technical conditions to rescue New Yorkers," he later wrote on X.

The Brooklyn building was built in 1930, city records show, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

articles.title: Father who beheaded three children among two men set for execution in US
articles.summary: Two men in the United States were scheduled to be executed on Thursday, including a Texas man convicted of beheading three young children he was raising
articles.body: Two men in the United States were scheduled to be executed on Thursday, including a Texas man convicted of beheading three young children he was raising in a 2003 crime that shocked a community along the US-Mexico border.According to news agency AP, in Oklahoma, James Pavatt was also due to receive a lethal injection for the 2001 murder of an advertising executive who was the estranged husband of a woman with whom Pavatt was having an affair. Prosecutors alleged that Pavatt and the woman, Brenda Andrew, planned and carried out the killing together. Andrew is currently the only woman on Oklahoma's death row.The executions come as the US is on course to record more than 40 executions for the second consecutive year, with Florida accounting for a significant share.The death penalty has also returned to the spotlight following California governor Gavin Newsom's recent announcement that he would commute hundreds of death sentences before leaving office. Experts have described the proposed move as potentially the largest mass clemency in US history.Pavatt, 73, was scheduled to be executed at the Oklahoma state penitentiary in McAlester, while John Allen Rubio, 46, was due to be put to death later in the day at the state prison in Huntsville, Texas.* Three children killed in TexasRubio and his girlfriend, Angela Camacho, were accused of murdering three children — three-year-old Julissa Quesada, 14-month-old John E Rubio and two-month-old Mary Jane Rubio — inside the poorly maintained, windowless apartment they shared in Brownsville, near the US-Mexico border.Camacho pleaded guilty to the killings and is serving a life sentence.Rubio's initial capital murder conviction was overturned by an appeals court, which ruled that statements made by Camacho had been improperly admitted as evidence during his trial. At his second trial, Rubio again pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity but was convicted and sentenced to death.Court records indicate that Rubio was not the biological father of the two older children but had raised them as his own.During different stages of the case, Rubio claimed that the children were possessed and described himself as the “chosen one” destined to save the world. Defence experts diagnosed him with paranoid schizophrenia, but prosecution experts disputed that assessment.Defence witnesses also testified that Rubio had endured a troubled childhood marked by domestic violence, abusive parenting, drug use and prostitution, which they said had affected his psychological development.The apartment building where the killings took place was subsequently demolished, and the site was converted into a park and community garden.* Oklahoma advertising executive killed in garagePavatt was convicted of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder in the 2001 killing of 39-year-old advertising executive Rob Andrew.Andrew was shot dead in the garage of his former home in Oklahoma City while collecting his two young children ahead of Thanksgiving.Pavatt, who attended the same church as the Andrew family, was having an affair with Andrew's wife, Brenda. The two were tried separately, convicted and sentenced to death.Several weeks before the murder, Rob Andrew had reportedly informed police that someone was trying to kill him after the brake lines of his car were cut.Following the shooting, Brenda Andrew told investigators that masked intruders had shot her in the arm and killed her husband.Pavatt and Brenda Andrew subsequently travelled to Mexico with her two children. They were arrested three months later while attempting to re-enter the United States.During a clemency hearing last month, Pavatt maintained that he was “not guilty of shooting anyone”. He said he had fallen in love with Brenda Andrew and had believed everything she told him.“It was not until my trial that I began to see the extent to which I had been manipulated by Brenda,” Pavatt told the clemency board. “I can see why the jury believed that we were both involved in Rob’s murder.”Prosecutors have maintained that Pavatt and Andrew conspired to kill Rob Andrew, arguing that both were equally responsible for the murder regardless of who actually fired the shots.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ukraine's power supply close to critical as Russian strikes bring darkness and cold
articles.summary: For parents in parts of Ukraine, trying to lead a normal family life with just a few hours of power each day is taking its toll.
articles.body:
Daryna Kulchytska is a mum under pressure. A single parent in a seventh floor flat in Kyiv trying to feed two lively kids and ensure they do their homework. But Daryna also faces the added strain of a deadline she can't even be certain of.

All she knows is soon the lights will go out, the sockets will lose power, the wi-fi will drop, and the taps will run dry. Tonight, the electricity has kept flowing an hour longer than advertised, but Daryna's still racing to serve dinner and finish her own work from home.

"The last few days it was only four or five hours we had power, but it's not at the same times. For two hours we have electricity, then for eight hours we don't."

As peace talks continue, with US envoys meeting the Russian and Ukrainian leaders on Thursday, Ukrainians are facing a rolling schedule of planned power cuts because of intensified Russian attacks on their energy grid. Ukraine has responded by striking Russian oil refineries.

Officials are concerned that life will quickly become unsustainable for millions of Ukrainians if power supplies cannot be maintained for at least four hours per day. Some privately warn that's close already, as some families are living with outages of up to 20 hours in Kyiv.

The power cuts were introduced earlier this year than last winter, and they're already lasting longer - making homes like Daryna's darker and colder. She's wrapped in layers of clothing and a heavy coat - the temperature is dropping, indoors and out.

Just before 7:30pm, there's a click and that's it - darkness until dawn.

The lift doesn't work, the water will stop flowing because electricity is needed to pump it to their flat. So the torches and LED candles come out and Daryna, her son Kyryll and daughter Olena gather for a card game of Uno before an early night.

Twelve-year-old Kyryll, speaking perfect English learned during two years living in the US, is frank about the disruption.

"There's no light, no water, no heat, no electricity. And no fun. All the fun got sucked out with the electricity," he says. "We have a lot of board games. We have a whole shelf, but we've played them like a hundred thousand times already."

Many families sit in the shadows as blackouts sweep entire neighbourhoods, smothering homes and streets in darkness.

"You look outside and sometimes you see nothing. You have a big city around but you see nothing because there's no light," Daryna says.

Kyiv has been worst hit - its metro trains and trolleybuses at times brought to a standstill. Nationwide, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians have gone without power in recent weeks.

We saw why on a visit to one of Ukraine's largest power stations, barely standing after a recent ballistic missile strike - the most powerful and devastating attack of Russia's campaign against Ukrainian energy targets.

The enormous plant - which we've been asked not to name for security reasons - has been reduced to a pile of twisted metal and broken pipes, its turbines buried in rubble, taking the site completely off line.

Volodymyr Kovalenko was on duty in the control room keeping the plant working when the missiles hit at 3am.

"It was a very powerful attack. We'd never experienced anything like it. We'd had strikes before – part of the roof had collapsed, it was pretty grim. But this time it was particularly severe."

Kovalenko, who followed in his parents' footsteps and has worked at the site for 25 years, says the damage is heartbreaking, though he's confident it can be repaired.

But the work is being hampered by air raids every 15-30 minutes – seven times during our four-hour visit. Each warning of drones and further missiles forces teams to down tools and dive for cover, though during our visit all were shot down or flew on towards other targets.

If there isn't time to reach the site's main shelter, the workers hide in the foundations of its towering chimneys.

"It's very difficult," says Vadym Bobyr, who is leading the recovery effort. "You've mentally prepared yourself to do a particular job, and then… the air raid siren goes off, and you have to get out as quickly as possible."

The 39-year-old, who has worked here half his life, is dwarfed by the mangled ruins and daunted by the challenge of rebuilding the plant.

"It's emotionally difficult, because we've already repaired all this, got it running again, and now it's happened all over again. It hurts, but we keep working and getting things done."

As we speak there's another alert - an incoming Banderol cruise missile.

The workers dart through the maze of passages and pipework but there isn't time to reach a shelter - one of the plant's thickest walls will have to do for cover. The missile was eventually intercepted 5km (3 miles) away.

Energy workers are at enormous risk. Since August there have been almost daily attacks on power facilities, claiming several lives every week. And it's getting more dangerous.

On the edge of the site, with the latest threat over, a team returns to reinstating the power lines feeding the national grid. But they won't be carrying electricity from the shattered plant before the end of this winter, at least.

President Volodymyr Zelensky says Ukraine still has enough generating capacity to meet electricity demand - the problem is getting it to homes and businesses when so many power lines and substations have been hit. Russia is using "waiter drones" that cling to pylons and cables and go undetected until Russia decides to detonate them.

Maxim Timchenko, CEO of DTEK, Ukraine's largest private energy company, said Russia was already putting the degraded electricity grid under even greater pressure than last year, and that overstretched air defences were unable to protect all of Ukraine's critical infrastructure.

"What is different is the scale of attacks and the different types of weapons used in these attacks. This is what is the difference - they've doubled in power and in scale".

He said rebuilding the damaged power station would take at least until next summer, because workers under sustained attack were limited to only one or two productive hours per day.

"We are fighting for survival of not only the whole country but ordinary people, especially during winter," Timchenko says.

Kovalenko echoes the sense of mission about trying to keep the lights on. "Energy is the foundation of everything - people's lives, the state. Nothing can function without it. I've dedicated my entire life to this".

Many are choosing to leave the capital, or Ukraine altogether, to avoid months of bitter cold. Daryna, Kyryll and Olena know the winter has barely begun.

"It's the worst feeling," Kyryll says. "When I get home from school, I'm tired. I lay in my bed. Bam! Air alarm. Bam! No lights. Bam! A lot of homework. Bam!"

When the children are in bed Daryna confides her thoughts of moving to somewhere safer, or warmer. She's torn by the desire to stay at home - close to friends and relatives - and the worry of how unbearable life may become.

The strain is damaging her mental health, she tells me, and she fears the impact on Kyryll and Olena, who suffers nightmares. Still, Daryna remains defiant despite the darkness.

"I don't want to live without light. But actually people in Ukraine say, OK, without light, but without Russians. Yes, we're scared, we're scared a lot. But better for us to be without power, but [also] without Russians."

articles.title: River Tyne nurdle spillage research to continue for a year
articles.summary: Research will be carried out on sea-birds and marine life following a microplastic spillage in July.
articles.body:
Research into the effects of a microplastic spillage on sea-birds and marine life will be carried out for the next year after funding was secured.

A team working across Tyneside is doing tests to discover the impact the pellets, known as nurdles, have on animals, birds and fish, as well as the overall spread.

Tonnes of microplastics were spilled into the River Tyne on 19 July following a collision between ships at the Port of Tyne.

North East England Beached Bird Surveys co-ordinator Dan Turner, who is leading the research on dead sea-birds, said: "This will be a long-term issue, securing the grant now gives us room to conduct more research not just in the North East but worldwide."

The research, which has been funded by The National Environment Research Council (NERC), will focus on the effects of the spillage on the River Tyne and at the coast.

Necropsies have been carried out on dead sea-birds at the Dove Marine Laboratory in Cullercoats, North Tyneside, for the past six weeks. The current stage is focusing on stomach rinsing, which will check if nurdles have been found in the birds' stomachs.

"We haven't found any evidence of plastics in the stomachs just yet but we have more to check and have evidence that nurdles have been found in regurgitated material," Turner said.

The research was prompted over concerns birds could "starve" if they confuse the nurdles for food and fill their stomachs.

"It's concerning plastics can also break down over time which could have a big effect on the wider food chain as well," Turner added.

The research team is being led by a team of scientists and experts at Newcastle University and the University of Liverpool.

They are also being assisted by volunteers and other regional organisations such as Environment Agency, Tyne Rivers Trust and Groundwork North East and Cumbria.

Over the course of the year the research will also look to map the travel of the plastic pellets.

The nurdles have been found in beaches across Tyneside, Wearside and Teesside, with experts suggesting they may have reached the coast of Denmark.

Dr Geoffrey Abbott, a reader in geochemistry at Newcastle University, said: "We hope to visit Denmark to determine if the pellets found are the nurdles from the Port of Tyne spill.

"There have been cases where they can travel great distances, for instance a spill in South Africa led to nurdles washing up in Perth, Australia, in no time at all."

Members of the public are being asked to continue to send pictures of nurdles to help with the research.

articles.title: Elmbridge Borough Council disposed of 2,300 artworks since 2021
articles.summary: The Surrey borough says nearly 17,000 works remain in its collection but only one is on display.
articles.body:
A council in Surrey has disposed of more than 2,000 works of art since 2021.

Elmbridge Borough Council said it had disposed of 1,436 items from its collection in 2021-22 and a further 927 the following financial year. None have been disposed of since 2023-24.

A council spokesperson said 25 items that "weren't relevant to Elmbridge" were sold for £319 and the rest were passed on to other organisations.

"We periodically review our collection so we can continue to collect and preserve items that tell the story of Elmbridge," they said.

The works sold in August 2022 included a line drawing of a World War One soldier from 1927, some watercolour portraits of women and watercolours of various flora and birds.

The spokesperson said: "Where an item is identified for disposal, we first consider whether it can have a new life through our learning resources.

"If not, we seek to pass it to another museum or an appropriate not-for-profit organisation, such as a theatre or home education group."

The figures, from a Freedom of Information request by the BBC, showed 16,819 works remained in the council's collection with only one on display as of April.

The authority said the art was among the 40,000 objects in the Elmbridge Museum collection, which includes archaeology, geology and social history exhibits.

The artwork collection was comprised of nearly 15,700 photographs, more than 1,000 works on paper such as sketches, 50 oil paintings and 14 sculptures.

The council spokesperson said the museum took collections "out into the community through displays, exhibitions, school learning resources, outreach activities and our digital channels".

"We currently have five physical displays at locations across Elmbridge and regularly rotate objects to explore different periods, events and stories from our local history," they said.

A BBC investigation found that across England, as of April, less than 5% of council-owned art was on display.

This is based on comparable Freedom of Information disclosures from 225 out of 316 English councils.

Elsewhere in Surrey, Epsom and Ewell, Mole Valley, Spelthorne, Tandridge and Woking councils reported having a handful of artworks.

Reigate and Banstead Borough Council said it had 103 works, a quarter of which were displayed.

Surrey Heath Borough Council reported owning 400 works.

The local authority said it rotated the paintings on public display at its offices and the Surrey Heath Museum, with an average of 31 on display at any one time.

"We are also in the process of making our painting collection available online to further improve accessibility," said a spokesperson.

articles.title: Kidney donation: I saved a stranger's life and also my husband's
articles.summary: Una Brown had always said she would give a kidney to her husband Sean if the time came, and she did so in a roundabout way.
articles.body:
By saving a stranger's life, Una Brown also saved her husband's.

Sean Brown was living with kidney failure and needed a transplant, but Una was not a 100% match.

The Belfast couple jumped at the chance to take part in the UK Living Kidney Sharing Scheme , which saw Una donate to a stranger, enabling Sean to receive a compatible organ from a different donor.

"When I was told that I wasn't a 100% match, you're automatically thinking, 'God, what's going to happen next?'

"But the fact that I could go into that sharing scheme – I had absolutely no issue with that.

"At the end of the day, if you actually think about it, two lives were saved in one day. It was the best decision of my life."

Sean had received his first kidney transplant aged eight – he was the face of an organ donation campaign as a child – but he always knew he might need another one in the future.

From the outset of their relationship, Una said she would give him one of hers when the time came.

"Immediately I just said - 'If you ever need a new kidney transplant, I'm going to donate' - without hesitation," she said.

Twenty-one years later, that is exactly what she did, in a roundabout way.

Sean had lived "an amazing life" for 37 years before the kidney's function started to deteriorate.

The couple entered the sharing scheme in July and the next month, Una received the news that a suitable match had been found.

"You can imagine that moment of just sheer relief," the 49-year-old council worker said.

"I genuinely cannot tell you what that felt like because it was the most emotional moment of my life.

"I knew there was hope and I knew Sean's life was going to get saved."

Sean, 45, received a call around the same time, bringing a "whirlwind of emotion".

The couple were initially included in a three-way transplant arrangement involving donors and recipients in different parts of the UK.

However, on the morning of surgery on 8 October, while Una was prepped for theatre, they received news that Sean's intended donor had become unwell and could no longer participate.

"I just looked at Sean and I saw his face. I thought, my God, his whole world was just crashing down around him," she said.

After an agonising wait, an alternative match emerged.

"By some miracle", Una said, the donor originally linked to her recipient was also compatible with Sean, allowing the transplant to proceed through paired donation.

Una's kidney was flown to Edinburgh, while Sean's donor kidney travelled to Belfast.

Hannah Magowan, one of the specialist transplant surgeons at Belfast City Hospital, who performed Sean's transplant and helped with Una's surgery, said the sharing scheme had been operating in Northern Ireland since 2010.

She said it had helped almost 200 people here receive a living-donor transplant.

In 2025/26 alone, 20 of the 69 living-donor kidney transplants took place through the scheme - almost three in every 10.

Magowan said Northern Ireland had become the biggest subscribers and contributors to the scheme, despite accounting for about 3% of the UK population.

She said Belfast was described as the "capital" of kidney sharing because of the number of patients and donors coming forward.

However she added there was probably a lack of awareness about the sharing scheme as "another method of donation", even among people living with kidney disease.

Magowan said living-donor transplants could help patients avoid dialysis, as in Sean's case, and potentially lengthy waits for a deceased-donor kidney.

"It's the gift of life for someone who can't avail of a direct donation," she added. "That's sharing at its best."

Sean and Una are recovering well and intend to return to work before Christmas.

Una wanted to reassure people that she would soon be back leading a "perfectly normal" life with just one kidney.

"We're now looking to the future and if Sean gets another 37 years we'll be doing very, very well," she added.

Una said she would never know much about who received her kidney other than they were critically ill and the transplant was successful.

"You don't need to know someone to change their life," she said.

"That's the gift of life through the sharing scheme – the fact that you are making that difference."

Sean could not put into words how he felt about his wife, who had given him "the gift of life again".

He hopes their "phenomenal journey" will encourage more people to consider living donation.

A 29-year-old man has been arrested after seven women reported being sexually assaulted in and around the University of Huddersfield's grounds.

West Yorkshire Police said it attended the university on Tuesday evening after being called by its security office and established all of the incidents happened between 18:00 and 18:30 GMT.

A spokesperson for the force said the women "had made off from a suspect after he approached and grabbed at them", with the arrested man remaining in police custody.

Det Insp Sarah Bradley said: "We fully recognise the distress and concern this incident has caused and can confirm a comprehensive investigation remains ongoing.

articles.title: Art trail celebrates arrival of black bears at Jersey Zoo
articles.summary: Jersey Zoo says the art trail will celebrate the world's "largest inhabitants to its smallest.
articles.body:
A new public art trail will mark the arrival of Asiatic black bears, Jersey Zoo has said.

Sculptures of bears and bees would be put up across the island's wild landscapes, coastal spots and urban spaces to celebrate the arrival of the new species in their new enclosure next year, said bosses.

They said the installation, which launches in July next year, aimed to shine a light on "connections that sustain the natural world, from its largest inhabitants to its smallest".

Artists will be invited to submit designs to turn the sculptures into "distinctive works of art" while schools and community groups will also be encouraged to participate.

It is hoped the sculptures will then be sold a fundraising auction at the end of the summer.

Rebecca Brewer, chief executive of Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust, said: "We want everyone who connects with our work, whether at Jersey Zoo or through our conservation projects around the world, to feel they can make a difference for nature.

"Our public art trails are a wonderful way to bring that belief to life."

She said previous Go Wild Gorillas and Tortoise Takeover trails "brought so much joy to Jersey, encouraging people to explore parts of the island they might never have visited, walk new paths, meet new people and create lasting memories".

An auction of the 54 tortoise sculptures raised £720,000 for a new tropical house.

articles.title: Handwritten 200-year-old dismissal letter found on Rugeley roof tile
articles.summary: The tile informs a worker that he is no longer needed and was signed by Thomas Austin.
articles.body:
What appears to be a 200-year-old letter of dismissal, written on a roof slate, has been found at a salvage yard.

The tile, informing what is thought to be a 19th-century pottery worker that he was no longer needed, was found at Cawarden Reclaim in Rugeley, Staffordshire

The message had been written into soft clay before the Staffordshire Blue tile was fired, and reads: "I do hereby discharge you, John Lewis, from my employment, Thomas Austin."

Research had found a firm called Thomas Austin Brick & Tile Makers, based at Clay Hills, Stoke-on-Trent in 1820, which could be the business referenced on the tile, the firm said.

"We were looking around and we just happened to come across this tile," said general manager Adam Giles.

He said he brought it back to his yard, cleaned it up a bit, and immediately felt it had a historic significance.

The name, location and period made a fascinating potential connection, the company said, but conceded they did not know for certain that the two were linked.

"If it is the same person [Thomas Austin], we may have uncovered not only a glimpse into somebody's working life in the early 19th century, but also a connection to the people who made the very building materials that have survived to this day," Giles said.

"You come across quite a few pawprints from animals and old shoes, where they used to walk across the clay while they were being fired," he said.

"You see that, but not very often you see handwritten text in a tile. Very unusual, very rare."

Once the inscription had been made, the clay was fired to create a finished roof tile and was then put to its intended use.

"The fact that someone went to the trouble of writing that out on the back of clay before it was fired, and then firing the tile and using it for the purpose it was designed for," Giles added.

The company said intriguing items such as this were uncovered from time to time, and that they were kept aside and preserved when they were found.

Eventually, they would go on display in the firm's reception area as part of a wall of interest, they said.

articles.title: Jersey gas bills to rise as Middle East turmoil persists
articles.summary: Gas bills will increase by about 5% from 1 December, Island Energy announces.
articles.body:
Gas customers in Jersey will see their bills increase by about 5% from 1 December after Island Energy announced a rise in tariffs for households and businesses.

The company said its mains gas, mini bulk tank and cylinder tariffs would increase by 1p per kilowatt hour (kWh) for all domestic and commercial customers from 1 December 2026.

It said the increase reflected higher wholesale gas and liquefied petroleum gas costs amid disruption to exports and shipping routes in the Middle East after the conflict with Iran.

Chief executive Graeme Millar said: "We recognise that any price increase is unwelcome, particularly during winter."

Securing fuel at lower prices in advance had limited the impact of wholesale cost increases on customers, Millar said.

However, the energy boss added: "It cannot fully protect customers from sustained increases in the cost of fuel and bringing it to Jersey."

Island Energy said customers concerned about paying their gas bills could contact its customer team to discuss what support might be available.

articles.title: Jeff Bezos' father fled Cuba with 3 shirts at 16; 33 years later, he and his wife invested $250,000 of their savings in Amazon, a bet that could now be worth more than the GDP of 100 countries
articles.summary: At 16, Miguel Bezos left Cuba for the United States with just three shirts, three pairs of trousers, a pair of shoes and a handmade jacket.
articles.body: At 16, Miguel Bezos left Cuba for the United States with just three shirts, three pairs of trousers, a pair of shoes and a handmade jacket. Arriving as an unaccompanied teenager during a period of political upheaval in Cuba, he had to rebuild his life in a country where he did not even speak the language. Over the next three decades, he completed his education, established a career in engineering and management, and started a family. In 1995, 33 years after leaving Cuba, he and his wife, Jackie Bezos, invested nearly $250,000 of their hard-earned savings in their son Jeff Bezos' fledgling online bookstore, Amazon, despite being warned that they could lose the entire amount. That early investment, based on subsequent stock splits and assuming the original shares were retained, could be worth more than $90 billion today, exceeding the annual GDP of more than 100 countries.Jeff Bezos’ father fled Cuba as a teenager under Operation Pedro PanBorn in Santiago de Cuba, Miguel Bezos left his home country in 1962 as part of Operation Pedro Pan, a programme that enabled thousands of Cuban children to travel to the United States without their parents. The migration took place amid concerns among Cuban families about the political changes following Fidel Castro's rise to power. Many parents believed sending their children to America would give them access to better opportunities and a safer future.Miguel arrived in Miami on July 21, 1962, at the age of 16. According to an account published by Amazon, he carried three shirts, three pairs of trousers, a pair of shoes and a handmade jacket. His mother had made the jacket using cleaning cloths because the family had limited resources.He initially stayed at Camp Matecumbe, a refugee centre in Florida, before being transferred to a Catholic institution in Wilmington, Delaware. His parents expected their separation to be temporary, but Miguel had to begin adapting to an unfamiliar country, a different culture and a language he did not know.From a refugee camp to a career at ExxonMiguel continued his education in the United States, attending Salesianum School in Wilmington, Delaware. He later received a scholarship to the University of Albuquerque in New Mexico, where he studied mathematics and graduated in 1968.During his university years, he met Jacklyn Gise, known as Jackie. The couple married in 1968. Jackie already had a son, Jeff Bezos, from her previous marriage. Miguel adopted Jeff when he was four years old, becoming his father and helping raise him.After graduating, Miguel built a professional career in engineering and management at Exxon. He worked for the energy company for more than three decades, taking up positions that provided financial stability for his family. His experience as an immigrant who had rebuilt his life through education and professional work would later form an important part of the Bezos family's story.How Jeff Bezos' parents invested nearly $250,000 in AmazonIn 1994, Jeff Bezos decided to leave his job at investment firm D E Shaw and pursue an opportunity he saw in the rapidly expanding internet. He moved to establish an online bookstore, which would eventually become Amazon.His parents became among his earliest financial backers. In February 1995, Miguel personally invested $100,000 in the company. A separate investment of $145,500 followed in July 1995 through Jackie's family trust. Together, their contributions amounted to approximately $245,500, commonly rounded to $250,000.The decision involved a considerable financial risk. Jeff later recalled warning his parents that there was a 70% chance they could lose their entire investment. He also remembered that his father initially asked him what the internet was, as the technology was still unfamiliar to many people at the time.Despite the uncertainty, Miguel and Jackie decided to support their son. Jeff later explained that his parents were investing in him rather than simply betting on the idea of an online bookstore. Their decision came at a time when Amazon was still a small start-up with no guarantee of becoming a successful business.Amazon's growth transformed the value of its early sharesAmazon launched its online bookstore in July 1995, initially selling books to customers through its website. The business expanded rapidly, receiving orders from all 50 US states and 45 countries within its first 30 days.The company went public in May 1997 at $18 per share, raising approximately $54 million. Over the following years, Amazon expanded beyond books into electronics, clothing, cloud computing, entertainment and other services, becoming one of the world's largest technology companies.Its growth also increased the potential value of shares acquired by its earliest investors. Amazon carried out four stock splits: a 2-for-1 split in 1998, two additional splits in 1999, and a 20-for-1 split in 2022. Together, these increased the original share count 240 times.The stock splits meant that early shareholders who retained their holdings would own substantially more shares than they originally purchased, although the value of each individual share adjusted accordingly.The value of the Bezos family's Amazon investmentBased on the original share purchases and the cumulative effect of Amazon's stock splits, the combined parental investment of approximately $245,500 could theoretically represent around 343.3 million shares.Using an illustrative Amazon closing price of $266.93 on November 9, 2026, the original combined shareholding would have a hypothetical value of approximately $91.63 billion, assuming all the original shares had been retained.The figure offers a striking comparison with the annual economic output of entire countries. According to World Bank data, Panama's nominal gross domestic product was approximately $90.46 billion in 2025. The hypothetical value of the original investment would therefore be slightly higher than Panama's annual GDP.At that valuation, the investment would also exceed the annual GDP of more than 100 countries and economies, depending on the GDP dataset and year used. The comparison illustrates the scale of Amazon's growth from a small online bookstore into a global technology business.Miguel and Jackie Bezos' philanthropic workBeyond their involvement in Amazon's early years, Miguel and Jackie Bezos also established a philanthropic presence through the Bezos Family Foundation, which they co-founded in 2000. The foundation supports initiatives focused on education, child development and opportunities for young people.The family has also donated substantial Amazon holdings over the years. Reports have documented transfers of Amazon shares to the foundation between 2001 and 2016, reflecting the couple's involvement in philanthropic activities as the company grew.Miguel's journey from an unaccompanied Cuban teenager arriving in America with a few belongings to an engineer, father and early Amazon investor has remained an important part of the history behind the company.You use AI every day. articles.title: UK economy grows at fastest rate for more than two years
articles.summary: ﻿The UK economy grew by 0.7% in the three months to September, according to official figures.
articles.body:
﻿The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.

Between July and September, the economy expanded by 0.7%, accelerating from the three months previously, official figures show.

The robust growth suggests a far more resilient economy than expected over the summer, despite the impact of higher energy prices from the Iran war.

Strong growth in the services sector - the largest part of the economy, which includes non-physical goods such as consultancy services and computer programming as well as hotels and restaurants - helped boost the numbers.

Within services, computer programming registered its fastest growth for the past three years, helped by AI linked spending.

The boost from computer programming and consultancy services has been the biggest driver of growth so far this year.

Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the Office for National Statistics, said it was "possible growth could have been even stronger" if there hadn't been a war in the Middle East.

But he says households may still not feel better off, and that prices might soon start to rise more quickly than wages.

However, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures were "welcome news".

He said: "Despite a year where events around the world have pushed up costs here at home, our economy is growing, bringing hope for the future.

The latest figures put the UK on course to be the second fastest growing economy across the major G7 countries which also includes Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France.

However, Jake Finney, senior economist at consultancy PwC, cautioned that growth was likely to slow over the coming months "unless energy markets stabilise".

A sharp rise in energy bills is forecast for January, which is likely to hit consumer spending and confidence, he said.

What's happening to the UK economy and how does it affect you?

Richard Benc, founder of mechanical watch company Studio Underdog, says sales are better than he expected.

"We've seen more resilience than we had forecast for and expected. We are still projecting growth this year," he says.

The business exports about 80% of its watches. "We've seen a surprising amount of resilience, particularly from our US customers," he adds, although some UK customers are now taking longer to buy watches.

articles.title: UK weather: Arctic air drops temperatures below zero as UKHSA issues cold health alerts
articles.summary: Colder than average conditions are spreading across the UK with overnight temperatures set to drop to -7C but the chilly snap may not last too long.
articles.body:
Northerly winds are sweeping across the UK, bringing cold air from the Arctic and some of the most widespread low temperatures of the autumn so far.

Thursday afternoon's highs will remain in single digits for most whilst overnight lows will widely fall below freezing, potentially dropping to -7C.

Strong winds will bring a significant wind chill, especially on northern and eastern coasts, so it will feel colder than the reading on the thermometer would suggest.

Yellow cold health alerts from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) have come into force.

Whilst the cold weather will come with sunshine in most areas, showers will also feature in northern parts of the UK, some of which could be wintry over high ground.

The first cold health alerts of the season cover the West Midlands and north-west England , external .

They have been issued by the UKHSA, in association with the Met Office, and are valid from now until 12:00 on Saturday.

The yellow alerts warn of minor impacts on the health and social care sector, with increased use of healthcare services by vulnerable people - who face a greater risk to life.

Heating tips to keep your home warm when budgets are squeezed

What are cold weather payments and who can get them?

The air affecting the UK on Thursday has come all the way from the Arctic.

It is a relatively clear air mass meaning plenty of sunshine and far less of the mist and fog that has plagued some areas recently.

Despite largely blue skies overhead, temperatures will struggle.

Afternoon highs are expected to range from 6 to 10C and the wind chill will make it feel colder than that.

The strongest winds will be in north-east Scotland where gusts will touch 50-60mph for a time. Blustery conditions will also affect the east coast of England and it will remain breezy elsewhere.

Showers will be blown into northern Scotland, falling as a mix of rain, sleet and hail - with a little snow possible over high ground.

This is not unusual for November as meteorological autumn draws into its final weeks.

Scattered showers will also affect Northern Ireland as well as northern and eastern England although the majority of these will be of rain.

Thursday night will be one of the most widely cold of autumn so far with temperatures forecast to drop below freezing in many areas.

As well as a widespread frost, a few icy stretches are possible - especially in northern Scotland.

Friday will bring more sunshine for many and generally lighter winds, although parts of northern Scotland will remain blustery.

Showers are most likely in Northern Ireland, Wales, north-west England and Scotland, where cloud amounts will tend to increase during the afternoon.

Friday night will deliver another frost for many areas and the weekend will stay generally chilly - although temperatures will gradually start to climb by a degree or two in both the day and night, as southerly winds develop.

Morning fog will become more of a feature again by Sunday morning and as high pressure starts to give way to low pressure and frontal systems, chances of rain will increase.

Next week looks more unsettled with stronger winds and rain at times.

Temperatures will, generally, be a little higher but incursions of cold air could continue to bring some wintry weather over Scottish mountains.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi and Nagina MP Chandra Shekhar Aazad on Thursday announced their alliance, Samajik Parivartan Morcha, for the 2027
articles.body: NEW DELHI: AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi and Nagina MP Chandra Shekhar Aazad on Thursday announced their alliance, Samajik Parivartan Morcha, for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections, with Aazad being the candidate for chief minister.The two leaders made the announcement at a joint press conference in Lucknow, bringing together their parties ahead of the state polls.Azad said the coalition was open to other parties, including the Samajwadi Party and Congress, if they wanted to contest the elections in support of the alliance to prevent the BJP from returning to power in Uttar Pradesh, PTI reported.Rejecting the description of the grouping as a "third front", Azad said it could become a political platform for deprived, oppressed and marginalised sections of society."People have been calling it a third front, but it is not a third front. It is the Samajik Parivartan Morcha. If you understand its depth, you will realise that it is the first front," he said.He said the alliance aimed to bring together weaker and deprived communities and help them use their electoral strength to gain political power and address their concerns.Invoking B R Ambedkar, Azad described political power as the "master key" to resolving people's problems. He argued that communities without their own political organisations could not effectively safeguard their interests, regardless of their population.Azad also cited Ambedkar's formation of political organisations, including the Scheduled Castes Federation, the Indian Labour Party and the Republican Party of India, saying he had recognised that existing political parties would not adequately represent marginalised communities.He further alleged that successive governments had failed to fulfil promises to bring deprived communities into the mainstream, tackle poverty and prevent atrocities against them.While AIMIM has a limited electoral presence in Uttar Pradesh, Owaisi has influence among sections of the minority community. Azad has been seeking to expand his support base among young Dalit voters.Owaisi said that if he and his supporters had to die while fighting for the cause of the people, it would be a worthwhile sacrifice.Taking a swipe at Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, Owaisi said he would not become the chief minister of Uttar Pradesh and accused him of practising the politics of entitlement.The development comes after Owaisi's attempt to join the INDIA bloc's seat-sharing arrangement in Uttar Pradesh failed to materialise. articles.title: EU: 50 world leaders in Dublin for major European summit
articles.summary: Ukraine, AI and hybrid threats in Europe to dominate EU summits in Dublin.
articles.body:
Ukraine, AI and hybrid threats across Europe will dominate key EU meetings in Dublin on Thursday and Friday.

The talks on AI will be the first such discussion among EU leaders.

The Republic of Ireland is chairing the EU presidency until the end of the year and its main showpiece events, the European Political Community (EPC) and informal meeting of the European Council, are taking place this week.

The country has been preparing for the events for months, with gardaí (Irish police) carrying out the largest security and policing operation in the history of the state.

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) will support their Irish counterparts in policing the summit.

Even though officers from abroad will not be involved in frontline policing, gardaí (Irish police) said they are being supported by the PSNI, police from Latvia and Portugal and other international law enforcement agencies.

Parts of Dublin city centre are closed off and there has been widespread traffic disruption in city in recent days.

The state has also been dealing with a number of bomb threats, which have been hoaxes, on schools and media organisations in recent days.

On Thursday, about 50 international leaders will gather at the Convention Centre Dublin for a meeting of the EPC.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham is expected to attend as part of his efforts to form closer ties with Europe.

Other attendees will include Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, heads of state across the EU as well as Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney.

The EPC is an informal forum for European leaders to hold political and strategic discussions on issues of shared concern.

It was set up in 2022 after Russian's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and meets twice a year.

The theme of the summit in Dublin is "Europe – strong, secure, and connected".

Leaders will discuss economic security, Ukraine, hybrid activity in Europe and democratic resilience.

Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.

Separately the taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Michéal Martin and the Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky have indicated that they may cooperate on the production of unmanned drones.

The two leaders met in Dublin on Wednesday ahead of a meeting of European leaders on Thursday.

Martin will greet his guests for a formal welcome on Thursday morning before the plenary session takes place.

All EPC leaders will then attend a dinner at the National Gallery of Ireland.

It is believed there will be a "handful" of no-shows, including Turkey as it is hosting the COP31 climate summit.

There will also be a meeting of a Friends of Ukraine group, co-hosted by the UK and Ukraine on the margins of the EU meeting, where Zelensky is expected to brief the leaders.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are expected to meet Zelensky in Dublin this week following trilateral talks on ending the war in Ukraine.

Kushner made the announcement after Ukraine and Russia finished their second day of US-brokered negotiations in Abu Dhabi.

It is understood that meeting is not part of the EU meetings happening this week.

On Friday, a meeting of the informal European Council will take place, also in the Convention Centre.

AI and Ukraine are the two issues due to dominate the event, with the so-called "godfather of AI" Prof Geoffrey Hinton among the speakers.
